university: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

documents.title: Student Generative AI Usage Guidance (UNC AI Committee)
documents.summary: The UNC Generative AI Committee, set up by the Provost and Deans, offers recommended syllabus language for instructors. It sets default principles (AI should help you think; you are responsible; use must be declared and documented), gives assignment-type guidance that mostly allows documented use, bans AI on exams unless the instructor permits, and leaves instructors free to override per assignment.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates: the cover note asks instructors to 'review and incorporate the recommended language in your syllabi, adapting them as you choose', and the guidelines apply 'Unless I provide other guidelines for an assignment or exam'. The document supplies a default framework but the instructor decides for the course; it is not a single university rule and has no named tiers.

units.why: States who made the guidance and how: 'the Provost and Deans created the UNC Generative AI Committee, with representatives from every academic unit'. That is a statement of origin and process, so P84.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=all, B=admin. The cover note says the Provost and Deans created the committee; it describes the institution's own set-up, not a rule addressed to everyone, so actor is admin (B).
units.anchor: the Provost and Deans created the UNC Generative AI Committee

units.why: The committee supplies 'recommended language' for instructors' syllabi; it is a template supplied by the institution, so P110 (sample syllabus language) rather than P56, which is about principles. Addressed to the institution's instructors via the cover note.
units.anchor: The UNC AI Committee has developed the following recommended language for student guidelines

units.why: The committee's premise that AI use is 'inevitable' acknowledges that AI cannot be prevented, which is why it is a limit-on-control statement (P82), not a rule.
units.resolution_why: Found by coder A only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'The view of the committee is that society's acceptance and use of generative AI is inevitable.' A real statement of the committee's premise that AI use cannot be stopped; kept as P82 with a fit note that it speaks of society's adoption and not of detection.
units.anchor: society’s acceptance and use of generative AI is inevitable
units.fit_note: Says society's adoption of generative AI is inevitable; P82 is about use that cannot be prevented or verified, so this fits only partly.

units.why: 'Organizations will expect our students to have generative AI skills' is the career argument for learning AI use, so P44. The learning/productivity/creativity benefit in the same sentence is coded separately as P87.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=neutral, B=encourage. The sentence gives the career argument ('Organizations will expect our students to have generative AI skills') and sets no rule on use. Rationale is neutral under the codebook, so A's neutral stands over B's encourage.
units.anchor: Organizations will expect our students to have generative AI skills

units.why: Names benefits ('useful tools for learning, productivity, and creativity') without making a rule or a career claim, so P87.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=neutral, B=encourage. 'will find them useful tools for learning, productivity, and creativity' names a benefit and states no rule; neutral (A), not encourage (B).
units.anchor: will find them useful tools for learning, productivity, and creativity

units.why: The guiding principle that AI 'should help you think. Not think for you' says students stay the primary thinker, so P32. It is stated as a philosophy (informs).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=student, B=all; anchor/policy wording. The sentence is the committee's guiding philosophy ('humans are responsible for the use of generative AI and that AI should help you think'), addressed to everyone who uses the guidance rather than to students alone; actor is all (B).
units.anchor: AI should help you think. Not think for you.

units.why: Asks instructors to put the language into syllabi ('Please review and incorporate ... in your syllabi'), a request rather than a mandate, hence should. Closest type is P09 (AI statement in the syllabus).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=neutral, B=permit; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Please review and incorporate the recommended language in your syllabi, adapting them as you choose to fit your course.' B's anchor already includes the adapt clause, so the anchor states the request and policy is null. It asks for adoption of template text and takes no position on AI use, so neutral (A), not permit (B).
units.anchor: incorporate the recommended language in your syllabi, adapting them as you choose
units.fit_note: Phrased as a request to adopt the committee's language and adapt it, not a requirement to have a statement. | Recommendation to adopt and adapt template language, not a mandate that every syllabus carry an AI statement.

units.why: Recommends covering the guidelines on 'the first day of class', i.e. going over the rules with students beyond printing them, so P66 (explain and discuss the rules).
units.anchor: It is also recommended that you cover them on the first day of class.
units.fit_note: Only says to cover the guidelines on day one; no mention of reasons or discussion. | Recommends covering the guidelines on day one; it does not say to give reasons or discuss, which P66 centers on.

units.why: The instructor 'can have different guidelines for a specific assignment or exam', so the rule is set per assignment by the instructor: P04.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on phase: A=during-work, B=before-course; unit_stance: A=permit, B=neutral; anchor/policy wording. The cover note tells instructors they 'can have different guidelines for a specific assignment or exam'. It is addressed to instructors when they set up their syllabus, so phase is before-course (B). It delegates the decision and takes no position, so unit_stance is neutral (B), not permit (A); A's fuller anchor is kept.
units.anchor: as the course instructor you can have different guidelines for a specific assignment or exam

units.why: Says the guidelines will 'continue to evolve' and (next sentence) invites feedback: a revisit statement, P54.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=admin, B=all. 'we expect these guidelines to continue to evolve' is the committee speaking about its own guidance, so actor is admin (A).
units.anchor: we expect these guidelines to continue to evolve

units.why: Names a contact person and the academic-unit representatives for questions and feedback on the guidelines, i.e. who owns and answers for the policy: P80.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=all, B=instructor; anchor/policy wording. The contact line sits in the note headed 'To the Instructor', so it is addressed to instructors (B). A's fuller anchor is kept and states the policy alone.
units.anchor: if you have any questions or feedback, please contact Mark McNeilly
units.fit_note: A contact for questions and feedback, not an enforcement or exception office. | Names a contact person and unit representatives for questions and feedback.

units.why: The first limitation notes that 'how output is arrived at is not clear' since internal processes cannot be determined; this is a caution about opacity of AI that does not match a type exactly, nearest P31 (verify output).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on policy_type: A=P31, B=UNCOVERED; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'how output is arrived at is not clear as the internal processes ... cannot be determined'. This is a warning about opacity of AI, not about wrong output, which is what P31 covers. A stretched it into P31 with a fit note; B called it UNCOVERED. Prefer UNCOVERED over a stretched fit, so UNCOVERED (B).
units.anchor: how output is arrived at is not clear
units.uncovered_note: Warns that AI output cannot be explained because its internal processes are opaque. | Also noted: Opacity of AI processes rather than wrongness of output.

units.why: States AI output 'may also be inaccurate or entirely fabricated', the core of P31.
units.anchor: may also be inaccurate or entirely fabricated, even if it appears reliable or factual

units.why: Says output 'may reflect biases that should be acknowledged', a bias concern with an obligation to acknowledge it, so P53.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on modality: A=should, B=informs. The sentence lists a limitation of AI ('may reflect biases that should be acknowledged'); the 'should' sits in a relative clause inside a description of the tool, so it informs (B), not should (A).
units.anchor: may reflect biases that should be acknowledged

units.why: 'AI evokes a range of intellectual property concerns; sourcing and ownership of information is unclear' raises ownership of AI output, which is P52.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=all, B=student. The limitation list describes AI in general to everyone reading the guidance, not students specifically; actor is all (A).
units.anchor: AI evokes a range of intellectual property concerns

units.why: Notes that the guidelines cover AI features built into everyday applications ('increasingly, generative AI capabilities will be integrated with everyday applications'), the embedded-AI scope of P07.
units.anchor: generative AI capabilities will be integrated with everyday applications
units.fit_note: A factual note on scope; no instruction about editors, IDEs or disabling features. | Notes AI is embedded in everyday applications and the guidelines cover those features, but sets no rule such as disabling them.

units.why: 'Unless I provide other guidelines for an assignment or exam, you should follow these guidelines' sets the fallback that applies when the instructor says nothing more specific (P06).
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'Unless I provide other guidelines for an assignment or exam, you should follow these guidelines.' A real fallback rule. B coded must but the source word is 'should'; modality should.
units.anchor: Unless I provide other guidelines for an assignment or exam, you should follow these guidelines.
units.fit_note: Fallback is these guidelines, not a ban or permit; it is what applies when the instructor's assignment rules are silent.

units.why: The principle's explanation lets students 'Use these tools to give you ideas, perform research ... and analyze problems', a permission for idea generation, so P15.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Use these tools to give you ideas, perform research (in compliance with point 2 below), and analyze problems.' A's anchor stops before 'analyze problems', so the anchor alone does not state the full permission; B's normalized policy is faithful and is used.
units.anchor: Use these tools to give you ideas, perform research
units.policy: Students use AI tools to give them ideas, perform research and analyze problems.
units.fit_note: Also permits research and analyzing problems, not only brainstorming. | Also permits research and problem analysis, wider than brainstorming.

units.why: 'Do not use them to do your work for you ... copy & paste the response as your answer' forbids having AI produce the submitted work: P19.
units.anchor: do not enter an assignment question into ChatGPT and copy & paste the response

units.why: Directs students to engage 'critically evaluating AI-generated outputs and considering potential biases', i.e. verify and evaluate output: P31.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Engage with AI technologies responsibly, critically evaluating AI-generated outputs and considering potential biases, limitations, and ethical implications'. A's anchor starts after 'Engage ... responsibly', so B's policy is used with A's fuller anchor.
units.anchor: critically evaluating AI-generated outputs and considering potential biases, limitations, and ethical implications
units.policy: Students engage with AI responsibly, critically evaluating AI-generated outputs and considering potential biases, limitations, and ethical implications in their analysis and discussions.

units.why: A general call to 'Utilize AI technologies ethically' naming privacy, confidentiality and IP without specific instructions, so P116.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on phase: A=general, B=during-work. 'Utilize AI technologies ethically, respecting privacy, confidentiality, and intellectual property rights' is a general ethical expectation under Usage Philosophy principle 2 and names no specific act or time, so phase is general (A).
units.anchor: Utilize AI technologies ethically, respecting privacy, confidentiality, and intellectual property rights.
units.fit_note: Names privacy, confidentiality and IP as areas but gives no concrete rule.

units.why: Requires data used with AI to be obtained and shared 'in compliance with relevant regulations', a compliance-with-law rule: P77.
units.resolution_why: Found by coder A only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'Ensure that the data used for AI applications is obtained and shared responsibly and in compliance with relevant regulations.' A real compliance rule; kept.
units.anchor: obtained and shared responsibly and in compliance with relevant regulations

units.why: 'You are 100% responsible for your final product' makes students own what they submit: P29.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on phase: A=general, B=during-work. 'You are 100% responsible for your final product' is a numbered principle of the philosophy, not tied to a stage of work; phase is general (A).
units.anchor: You are 100% responsible for your final product.

units.why: Tells students to delete AI content they cannot verify ('If you cannot verify it as factual, you should delete it'), a verify-output rule: P31.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on modality: A=should, B=must; unit_stance: A=neutral, B=restrict; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'If you don't know whether a statement ... is true, then your responsibility is to research it. If you cannot verify it as factual, you should delete it.' The source word is 'should', so modality is should (A), not must (B). Removing unverified AI content limits what may stay in submitted work, so unit_stance is restrict (B). 'it' is ambiguous in the anchor, so a policy is written.
units.anchor: If you cannot verify it as factual, you should delete it.
units.frag_start: If you don’t know whether a
units.policy: Students who do not know whether a statement in AI output is true research it, and delete it if they cannot verify it as factual.

units.why: 'The use of any AI ... must be declared in your submission and explained' is a mandatory disclosure with each submission: P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=permit. 'The use of any AI ... must be declared in your submission and explained' is a mandatory disclosure; unit_stance require (A), not permit (B).
units.anchor: must be declared in your submission and explained

units.why: Puts the duty on students to find out which rules apply ('It is your responsibility to ensure you are following the correct guidelines'), given instructors may set assignment-specific rules: P78.
units.anchor: It is your responsibility to ensure you are following the correct guidelines.

units.why: Students should not enter confidential or personal data (the text gives One Card details as an example) into AI tools: protect personal data, P50.
units.anchor: Data that are confidential or personal should not be entered into generative AI tools.

units.why: Explains that entering personal data 'exposes you and others to the loss of important information', which is the privacy reason for the preceding rule; same type as the rule (P50).
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'Putting confidential or personal data ... exposes you and others to the loss of important information.' The reason for the privacy rule; kept as informs.
units.anchor: exposes you and others to the loss of important information

units.why: Footnote: 'ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines' and 'Sentient Syllabus was a resource', disclosing how the guidance itself was made (P84).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on policy_type: A=P48, B=P84. Source (footnote): 'ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines'. P48 is about AI-made course materials; this discloses how the policy document itself was made, which is P84 (B).
units.anchor: ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines

units.anchor: Sentient Syllabus was a resource for a number of the ideas

units.why: Says AI tools 'can assist with brainstorming, finding information, and even reading and creating materials', a general acknowledgment of permitted uses (P15).
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'These tools can assist with brainstorming, finding information, and even reading and creating materials.' Acknowledges permitted uses; kept.
units.anchor: These tools can assist with brainstorming, finding information, and even reading and creating materials
units.fit_note: Lists several uses (finding information, reading, creating materials) beyond brainstorming.

units.why: 'you are responsible for the final product of your work, both academically and in the workforce' repeats ownership of submitted work (P29); not an exact repeat because it adds the workforce.
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'Regardless of your use of any AI tools, you are responsible for the final product of your work, both academically and in the workforce.' Not an exact repeat of principle 3 because it adds the workforce; kept.
units.anchor: you are responsible for the final product of your work, both academically and in the

units.why: Violating the guidelines 'may be a reportable violation to the UNC Honor Court', which routes misuse to the integrity process: P36.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=student, B=all; anchor/policy wording. 'Not following these guidelines may be a reportable violation to the UNC Honor Court' binds students who must follow the guidelines; actor student (A). B's fuller anchor states the whole rule, so policy is null.
units.anchor: Not following these guidelines may be a reportable violation to the UNC Honor Court.

units.why: Writing and presentation: 'you may submit material that contains AI-generated content' if documented, including drafting outlines and sections; this allows AI-generated text under a disclosure condition, nearest P18 (rules for prose), though the permission itself is closer to P91.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on policy_type: A=P16, B=P18; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Writing and Presentation: In principle, you may submit material that contains AI-generated content ... if this use is properly documented.' P16 covers AI-generated code; this passage is about prose and presentations, so P18 (B), kept with a fit note. The anchors stop before the documentation condition, so a policy is written.
units.anchor: you may submit material that contains AI-generated content, or is based on or derived from
units.policy: In principle, students may submit writing and presentation material that contains AI-generated content, or is based on or derived from it, if this use is properly documented.
units.fit_note: Applies to writing and presentation material, not code. | Allows AI-generated prose (outlines, sections, combining, annotating references) if documented; P18 has no sub-rule on documentation.

units.why: 'Your documentation must make the process transparent' requires disclosure of how AI was used in writing assignments: P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=neutral. 'Your documentation must make the process transparent' is a mandatory disclosure standard; require (A).
units.anchor: Your documentation must make the process transparent

units.why: For multimedia assignments students may submit AI-generated images, audio, music or video if documented, which is the images-and-graphics permission P106.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Multimedia Assignments: In principle, you may submit material that contains AI-generated content ... if this use is properly documented. This may include the generation of images, audio, music, video, etc.' The anchor omits the documentation condition, so B's policy is used.
units.anchor: This may include the generation of images, audio, music, video, etc.
units.policy: Students may submit multimedia assignment material containing AI-generated images, audio, music or video if the use is properly documented.
units.fit_note: Covers audio, music and video as well as images.

units.why: Lists math, statistical and data analysis and says 'Generative AI can be used for these purposes': the data-analysis permission P89.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Generative AI can be used for these purposes; however, the output must be verified ...'. 'these purposes' needs the preceding list, so a policy is written. The verification condition is its own rule (next unit), so it is left out of this policy; B's version merged two rules.
units.anchor: Generative AI can be used for these purposes
units.policy: Generative AI can be used for mathematical and statistical analysis, data analysis, data interpretation, coding of data and other forms of quantification of language or concepts.
units.fit_note: Verification condition is coded separately. | Adds the condition that output be verified by the student's own calculations with proof of work.

units.why: AI output in analysis 'must be verified via your own mathematical calculations and proof of work', a verification duty: P31.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=neutral, B=restrict; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'the output must be verified via your own mathematical calculations and proof of work provided in your assignment.' It is a verification duty, not a restriction on use, so neutral (A), not restrict (B). 'the output' is ambiguous in the anchor, so B's clarifying policy is used.
units.anchor: the output must be verified via your own mathematical calculations and proof of work provided
units.policy: For mathematical and statistical analysis and other data work with AI, the output must be verified via the student's own mathematical calculations and proof of work provided in the assignment.
units.fit_note: Also requires proof of the verification work in the assignment. | Requires proof of work in the assignment, beyond verifying.

units.why: Permits AI to 'analyze readings' as an aid to understanding material, closest to P12 (AI as a tutor for understanding), with the proviso in the next sentence.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on policy_type: A=P12, B=P14. Source: 'Generative AI can be used to analyze readings.' Analyzing assigned readings is using AI to understand material, closer to P12 than to P14 (practice and study aids). P12 (A) kept with the fit note that the permission is conditioned on also doing the readings.
units.anchor: Generative AI can be used to analyze readings.
units.fit_note: Permission is to analyze assigned readings, and it is conditioned on also doing the readings. | Permits analysis of readings; P14 is about practice and study aids, close enough.

units.why: Says AI analysis 'is not a substitute for reading the works themselves', so AI must not replace the student's own engagement; P32 fits best.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on modality: A=must-not, B=must; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'However, you must also do the readings. Generative AI analysis is not a substitute for reading the works themselves.' The anchored sentence says AI may not stand in for the reading, which is a prohibition on substitution, so must-not (A).
units.anchor: Generative AI analysis is not a substitute for reading the works themselves.
units.fit_note: Specific to readings: students must do the readings themselves.

units.why: 'participating in online discussions of readings requires that you provide your own contributions' means discussion posts must be the student's own (P29).
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'participating in online discussions of readings requires that you provide your own contributions.' A real rule on discussion posts; kept.
units.anchor: requires that you provide your own contributions

units.why: 'do not generate responses to readings using AI' unless the instructor allows is a ban on AI producing submitted responses: P19.
units.anchor: Unless I specifically allow it, do not generate responses to readings using AI.

units.why: 'you must account for and document your use' of AI in research is mandatory disclosure: P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=permit. 'you must account for and document your use' is a mandatory disclosure for research; require (A), not permit (B).
units.anchor: you must account for and document your use
units.fit_note: Applies disclosure to research stages (brainstorming, search assistance, source evaluation, summaries).

units.why: Lists research uses of AI (search assistance, source evaluation, summaries) as possibilities, which is the literature-and-sources permission P104.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Possibilities include topic brainstorming, search assistance, source evaluation, and summaries and source documentation.' The anchor lacks the research context, so a policy is written.
units.anchor: topic brainstorming, search assistance, source evaluation, and summaries and source documentation

units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=neutral. 'Track your use of AI throughout these stages, and then document this assistance as you submit' requires keeping and submitting a record; require (A).
units.anchor: Track your use of AI throughout these stages

units.why: AI-generated material 'should also be documented in your citations': citing AI use in the submission, P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=neutral; anchor/policy wording. 'Any material generated through AI in your projects should also be documented in your citations': the source says should; a citation duty on students, so require (A) as in the other disclosure units.
units.anchor: Any material generated through AI in your projects should also be documented in your citations.

units.why: For simulations students 'may use AI tools for advice or brainstorming': P15.
units.anchor: you may use AI tools for advice or brainstorming

units.why: Bars using AI in simulations to 'find cheats or other unfair advantages'. This is a specific prohibition on exploiting a simulation, which none of the types P19-P23 describes.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=restrict, B=prohibit. Source: Simulations: 'you may use AI tools for advice or brainstorming. It should not, however, be used to find cheats or other unfair advantages.' AI is allowed for narrow uses and barred for another, so restrict (A), not prohibit (B). UNCOVERED in both.
units.anchor: It should not, however, be used to find cheats or other unfair advantages.
units.uncovered_note: In simulation assignments, AI must not be used to find cheats or unfair advantages in the simulation. | Also noted: Bans using AI to find cheats or unfair advantages in simulations.

units.why: When AI names a source, students must 'find and attribute the original source of the idea' and give a working link, a check on AI-supplied sources (the text warns AI 'tends to invent sources'). P31 is nearest.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on policy_type: A=P31, B=P25; unit_stance: A=require, B=neutral; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'If a source is identified, find and attribute the original source of the idea, identify the location of the text within the source, and provide a working link ... If you are not able to locate the source, delete that content.' Both coders found a source-attribution duty that is not the same as citing the tool (P25) or just verifying (P31). P31 is the nearest type (A) because the text warns 'generative AI tends to invent sources'; fit note kept. unit_stance is require because it requires attribution. The delete clause is coded as its own unit.
units.anchor: find and attribute the original source of the idea

documents.title: Student Use Guidelines for Generative AI
tiers: Template A: no generative AI of any kind in the course (violations referred to the Honor System)
Template B: a listed set of permitted uses (e.g. topic selection, brainstorming, research, drafting, polishing), with attribution and a usage form
documents.summary: The College of Arts & Sciences adapts the university committee's guidance into student guidelines and an instructor cover note. It sets principles (AI should help you think; student is 100% responsible; use must be declared; no confidential data), and tells instructors to pick one of two syllabus statements: a full ban or a list of permitted uses with verification and a documentation form.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates: principle 2 says 'The rules for use of AI in particular courses are to be determined by the course instructor', and instructors are told to specify either a full ban or a list of permitted uses. The college offers two templates (tiers) and sets no stance of its own.

units.fit_note: Says society's adoption of generative AI is inevitable; P82 is about use that cannot be prevented or verified, so this fits only partly.

documents.title: Guidance on Generative AI Use (Graduate School Handbook)
documents.summary: The Graduate School Handbook page asks graduate programs to embrace the university committee's philosophy that humans are responsible for AI and that AI should help you think. It lets programs set their own thesis and exam rules, applies campus student and teaching guidance to graduate students and TAs, and lists discussion topics (disclosure, appendices, journal and funder rules, IP, data leakage) for students and advisors.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates: the Board 'encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy', says 'Individual graduate programs may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams', and frames research use as a topic to 'be discussed with supervisors, advisors'. It sets no ban or permission itself.

Source: 'the Administrative Board encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy guiding the recommended language'. It states a principle for the Graduate School, so general (A), not before-course (B). The anchor does not say what the philosophy is, so B's policy is used.
units.anchor: encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy guiding the recommended language
units.policy: The Graduate School's Administrative Board encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy guiding the recommended language that humans are responsible for the use of generative AI and that 'AI should help you think. Not think for you.'
units.fit_note: Addressed to programs; it encourages adopting the principle, not a rule for students.

units.why: Says AI 'can be a productive tool and foster new directions and perspectives' for teaching and research: a benefit statement, P87.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=all, B=admin; anchor/policy wording. 'The Board maintains that generative AI can be a productive tool' is the Board speaking; actor admin (B).

Source: 'the Board recognizes that embracing generative AI tools may have nuanced applications for graduate students, faculty advisors, and degree program administrators.' B called it P85, but it does not let units set rules; it only says graduate use differs. Prefer UNCOVERED over a stretched fit.
units.anchor: may have nuanced applications for graduate students, faculty advisors, and degree program administrators
units.frag_start: the Board recognizes that embracing generative AI tools
units.uncovered_note: Recognizes that generative AI may have nuanced applications for graduate students, faculty advisors and degree program administrators.

units.why: Programs 'may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams': units may set their own rules, P85.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=permit, B=neutral. 'Individual graduate programs may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams' delegates to programs and takes no position on AI use; neutral (B), not permit (A).
units.anchor: Individual graduate programs may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams

units.why: Where a program encourages AI, campus student-use guidance 'should also apply to graduate students in their own classes and research': it sets the scope of the university framework for graduate students, P56.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source includes the condition 'If generative AI use is encouraged in a program'; A's anchor omits it, so B's policy is used.
units.anchor: guidance developed for the campus related to student use should also apply to graduate students
units.policy: If generative AI use is encouraged in a program, guidance developed for the campus related to student use should also apply to graduate students in their own classes and research.
units.fit_note: Scope statement extending campus guidance to graduate students. | Applies campus student guidance to graduate students; no framework of its own.

units.why: Reminds students they 'are always subject to the UNC Student Code of Conduct', i.e. AI use falls under existing university policy: P77.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on modality: A=informs, B=should; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Students should remember that they are always subject to the UNC Student Code of Conduct.' A reminder of an existing rule, which is awareness and so informs (A), not a new command (should, B).
units.anchor: they are always subject to the UNC Student Code of Conduct

units.why: Campus teaching-use guidance 'should also apply to instructors, including teaching assistants', extending the institutional framework to TAs: P56.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on actor: A=instructor, B=ta-staff. 'should also apply to instructors, including teaching assistants': instructors are the main addressee, TAs are included; actor instructor (A).
units.anchor: should also apply to instructors, including teaching assistants
units.fit_note: Scope statement for instructors and TAs.

units.why: Programs can encourage TAs to connect with supervisors so that 'the supervisor supports the TA using AI in their own grading/teaching work': TA AI use in teaching depends on supervisor support, nearest P59.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on modality: A=may, B=should; policy_type: A=P59, B=P101; unit_stance: A=neutral, B=permit; anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Programs can encourage TAs to connect with supervising faculty to ensure any enrolled student usage complies with class guidelines and the supervisor supports the TA using AI in their own grading/teaching work.' The sentence has two rules. A anchored the second, B coded it as B9 (P101, grading) and the first as B8 (P109). The second is about TAs' AI use in teaching work generally, not only grading, so P59 (A) with A's fit note; TA use is permitted with supervisor support, so permit. The first rule is kept as its own unit (B8).
units.anchor: the supervisor supports the TA using AI in their own grading/teaching work
units.policy: Programs can encourage TAs to connect with supervising faculty to ensure the supervisor supports the TA using AI in their own grading/teaching work.
units.fit_note: Requires supervisor support for TA AI use in grading and teaching and compliance of student use with class guidelines. | Covers teaching work generally, not only grading, and makes supervisor support the condition.

units.why: Programs 'can encourage TAs to connect with supervising faculty to ensure any enrolled student usage complies with class guidelines', which asks TAs to align with the instructor (P109).
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'Programs can encourage TAs to connect with supervising faculty to ensure any enrolled student usage complies with class guidelines'. The first of two rules in one sentence (A anchored only the second). P109 (aligning TAs with the class rules) is B's choice and the nearest type; kept with its fit note.
units.anchor: encourage TAs to connect with supervising faculty to ensure any enrolled student usage complies
units.policy: Programs can encourage TAs to connect with supervising faculty to ensure any enrolled student usage complies with class guidelines.
units.fit_note: Aligns TA handling of student AI use with the supervising faculty's class rules.

units.why: Programs 'should share these resources and guidance' with TAs, directing them to the guidance: P115.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on phase: A=course-start, B=before-course. 'Graduate programs should share these resources and guidance with any graduate students serving as TAs' is institutional set-up before TAs teach; before-course (B).
units.anchor: Graduate programs should share these resources and guidance with any graduate students serving as TAs.
units.fit_note: Directs programs to pass AI guidance to TAs.

units.why: AI use in research and writing 'should be discussed with supervisors, advisors, committee members': an AI rule for graduate research, P62.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on anchor/policy wording. Source: 'Any use of AI for research and writing purposes should be discussed with supervisors, advisors, committee members, and any other associated individuals.' A's anchor lacks the subject, so B's policy is used.
units.anchor: should be discussed with supervisors, advisors, committee members, and any other associated individuals
units.policy: Any use of AI for research and writing purposes should be discussed with supervisors, advisors, committee members, and any other associated individuals.
units.fit_note: A duty to discuss AI use with advisors rather than deferring to venue rules. | Calls for discussion with advisors rather than deferring to external venue rules.

units.why: Warns AI use 'might lead to data leakage' and permanence of unverified data: a data-protection warning, P50.
units.anchor: use of AI might lead to data leakage and proliferation, permanence, and widespread availability

units.why: Suggests discussing 'order of writing and editing and using these tools, and how to incorporate its use and permissions for publishing' (P62).
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on policy_type: A=P90, B=P62. Source: a suggested discussion topic: 'Order of writing and editing and using these tools'. It does not say students draft before using AI (P90), only that the order is something to discuss in research and writing; P62 (B).
units.anchor: Order of writing and editing and using these tools
units.fit_note: Only a topic for discussion, not a rule that students draft before using AI.

units.why: Students and advisors should discuss journal and granting-agency AI policies, i.e. defer to venue and funder rules: P62.

units.why: Raises that journals 'may disallow submission of material that has been previously submitted to AI sites' as previously published: a copyright and ownership concern, P52.
units.anchor: certain journals may disallow submission of material that has been previously submitted to AI sites

units.why: Lists research stages (design, drafting, data analysis, media) that students should discuss with advisors regarding AI: governing AI in research, P62.
units.resolution_why: Found by coder A only; checked against the source and kept. Source: 'Discuss methods/development of research design, drafts and writing generation and editing, ...'. A real suggestion for discussion with advisors; kept.
units.anchor: Discuss methods/development of research design, drafts and writing generation and editing

units.why: Lists 'Citations and/or a statement disclosing specific uses of AI' as something to settle for research outputs: disclosure with the work, P24.

units.anchor: Citations and/or a statement disclosing specific uses of AI
units.fit_note: A discussion topic for research products rather than a fixed requirement.

units.why: Suggests an appendix documenting 'any exchanges (input or output ...) using AI', i.e. keeping and submitting the AI exchanges: P26.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=neutral; anchor/policy wording. A suggested discussion topic (appendix documenting exchanges), not a requirement; neutral (B), not require (A).
units.anchor: Include appendix documenting any exchanges (input or output of materials, texts, or data) using AI
units.fit_note: A discussion topic, not a fixed requirement.

units.why: Suggests a methods section 'explaining the use of AI and its impact on research/products', a disclosure inside the work: P24.
units.resolution_why: Coders differed on unit_stance: A=require, B=neutral. A suggested discussion topic (methods section explaining AI use), not a requirement; neutral (B), not require (A).

notes: Reconciled from two independent codings. Computing layer none-found and course layer deferred. UNC has three coded documents: the UNC AI Committee student guidance (hosted by the pharmacy school), the College of Arts & Sciences student guidelines (which reuse much of the committee wording; each text was coded on its own), and the Graduate School handbook page. Both coders left new_types empty. Opacity-of-AI limitations and the note that an AI citation is not a source for facts were coded UNCOVERED in both guideline texts. Fit and uncovered notes from either coder are kept on the units.
